# Apostille Atlas: full text

> State-by-state apostille fees, offices, and mail versus in-person rules, copied from official secretary of state pages, plus apostille versus authentication and online notarization.

# Apostille Atlas
A state-by-state guide to U.S. apostilles and authentication certificates: the official fee, the issuing office, mail versus in-person filing, and whatever processing time that office actually publishes.
An apostille is a certificate that authenticates the signature on a public document so the document can be used in another country that belongs to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention. The Hague Conference describes the Convention as replacing the longer legalization chain with a single apostille issued by a competent authority where the document originates. [source](https://www.hcch.net/en/instruments/conventions/specialised-sections/apostille)
We copy fees and rules from official government pages and put a source link on every claim. Offices change prices and counter hours. This is general information, not legal advice. We don't file documents ourselves, but if you'd rather hand the job off, our request form passes it to an independent apostille service.
Rather not do this yourself?
Tell us the document, the state that issued it, and where it's going. We'll pass your request to an independent apostille service that can handle the whole thing, and they'll reply with a quote. It's free to ask and you're under no obligation.

## State guides

### Apostille Done-Right Checklist Pack
Checklists, request letters and an order log for getting a document apostilled or authenticated the first time. $19, with a 14-day money-back guarantee.

### New York
$10 per document at the Department of State. Same-day walk-in service, limited to 10 documents, at five customer-service offices. No published mail turnaround.

### California
$20 per apostille by mail; in person add $6 special handling per public official’s signature. Sacramento was processing mail received November 12, 2026, as of November 20, 2026.

### Texas
$15 per universal apostille ($10, capped at $100, for an adoption). Same-day in-person service for up to 10 documents; mailed requests can take up to two weeks from receipt.

### Florida
$10 per document, or $20 when a clerk-of-court certification needs a certificate of incumbency. Walk-in service in Tallahassee; as of November 20, 2026, apostille requests received November 16, 2026 were being processed.

### Massachusetts
$6 per document. Up to three documents at the Boston counter; mailed requests are processed within two to three weeks. Regional offices in Springfield and Fall River.

### New Jersey
$25 standard or $40 expedited per document, ordered and prepaid online first. Standard mail service takes 12 to 20 business days; walk-in expedited service in Trenton.

### Virginia
$10 per document, $5 for extra same-signer documents. Documents must be dated within 12 months. Richmond is appointment-only, and eNotary documents can’t be authenticated.

### North Carolina
$10 per document. Walk-in service in Raleigh with no appointment; mailed requests generally take five business days longer. Foreign-language documents need a wet-signed English translation.

### Pennsylvania
$15 per document. Walk-in requests in Harrisburg are processed while you wait; mail takes 5 to 7 business days after receipt. Diplomas, transcripts, and criminal record checks must be notarized first.

### Missouri
$10 per notary or official on the document, capped at $100 per child for adoptions. Same-day walk-in service in Jefferson City and branch offices in St. Louis, Kansas City, and Springfield.

### Washington
$15 per document. Standard 7 to 10 business days, expedited 2 to 3 for $100 per 10 documents, or same day in Tumwater or Cheney for $150 per first 10.

### Michigan
$1 per document from the Office of the Great Seal. Mail to Lansing or book a visit at one of nine offices; no expedited service. Diplomas and copies need a signed “true copy” statement before a Michigan notary.

### Connecticut
Every order starts online. Paper apostilles take 5 to 7 business days after arrival in Hartford; e-Apostilles, about 24 hours. Documents must be signed or notarized in Connecticut within the last 10 years.

### Maryland
$5 per document. Notarized papers go to the Clerk of the Circuit Court in the notary’s county first. Mail takes 7 to 14 business days by regular mail, about 3 to 4 by courier or Priority Mail.

### Georgia
$3 per document from the GSCCCA in Atlanta, not the Secretary of State. Walk in with no appointment or mail it; mailed requests normally take one to two business days. Non-Hague countries need the Secretary of State’s Great Seal Certification.

### Colorado
$5 per apostille by mail or drop-off, $15 for expedited walk-in service in Denver, generally under an hour. Check or money order only; free document review by email before you submit.

### Minnesota
$5 per document, by mail or in-person appointment in Saint Paul. Minnesota issues only apostilles, for every country, and notarizations must show all six elements of Minnesota law.

### Arizona
$3 per document from the Secretary of State. Mail takes 10 to 20 business days; walk-in service in Phoenix or Tucson adds a $25 expedite fee and is limited to 6 documents. No electronic apostilles.

## How the certificate works

### Apostille by country
All 129 other Hague Apostille Convention countries, when the Convention took effect, whether it applies with the U.S., and who issues apostilles there. Thailand joins February 28, 2027.

### Apostille offices by state
The designated apostille authority in every state, D.C., and U.S. territory, with links to the states that let you verify an apostille online.

### How to verify an apostille
Only the issuing office can confirm an apostille. The 17 U.S. authorities with an online register listed by the Hague Conference, and what to do when there is no online search.

### Does an apostille expire?
No: under the Convention an apostille can’t be refused for its age. What can run out is the receiving country’s time limit on the document underneath.

### Apostille versus authentication
Hague Convention countries generally use an apostille. Non-Hague countries often need a different certificate, and sometimes a further step at the U.S. Department of State. States do not all issue the same kind of paper.

### Online notarization (RON)
A remote online notary can notarize a document, but the apostille still comes from the state competent authority. Texas publishes a specific RON checklist; some countries still refuse online notarizations.

## Official fees at a glance
These are the government fees published on each office’s own page, last checked November 22 to 28, 2026. They do not include county-clerk, certified-copy, notary, translation, courier, or embassy charges.

Home › Does an apostille expire?
# Does an apostille expire?
Short answer: No. Under the Hague Apostille Convention, a validly issued apostille stays in effect for as long as it can be identified and remains attached to its document, and it can’t be rejected just because of its age. But the country receiving the document can set its own time limit on the document underneath, for example requiring a record issued within a certain period. When people say an apostille “expired,” that is usually what happened. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf)

The Hague Conference’s Apostille Handbook (second edition, 2023) is the official practical guide to how the Convention works. It addresses the age question in three places: the general rule, the list of grounds on which an apostille may not be rejected, and the section on e-Apostilles. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf) [source](https://www.hcch.net/en/publications-and-studies/details4/?pid=5888)

## What the Convention rule actually says

| Question | Answer from the Apostille Handbook |
| Does the apostille itself have an end date? | No. It has effect for as long as it is identifiable and stays attached to the underlying public document. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf) |
| Can the receiving country reject an apostille as too old? | No. An apostille may not be rejected on the basis of its age. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf) |
| Can the receiving country require a recent document? | Yes. Contracting Parties may set time limits on accepting foreign public documents, for example that the document be produced within a certain period after it was executed. Those limits can’t be applied to the apostille itself. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf) |
| Can an expired document be apostilled? | Usually. Some documents carry their own validity period (criminal records, identity and travel documents, provisional court orders). Expiry doesn’t ordinarily stop them being public documents unless the law of the issuing country says so, and as long as it is still a public document it can be apostilled. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf) |
| Does an e-Apostille expire when the signer’s digital certificate does? | No. An e-Apostille stays valid after the signing official’s digital certificate expires, as long as that certificate was valid when the e-Apostille was issued. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf) |

The reason the rule works this way: an apostille only certifies where a public document came from, meaning the signature, the capacity of the person who signed it, and any seal or stamp. It doesn’t certify the content. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/6dd54368-bebd-4b10-a078-0a92e5bca40a.pdf) Whether the content is current enough is a separate question for the receiving authority, which keeps the right to decide whether a foreign document is admissible and what weight it carries. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf)

## Where age limits usually bite
The time limit almost always sits on the document, not the certificate. The Handbook itself names criminal records among the documents that carry their own validity period. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf) In practice that means:

- Criminal record checks carry their own validity period. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf) If the receiving office sets a limit on how recent the record must be, ask what it is before you order the check, so the time spent getting the apostille doesn’t use up that window.
- Vital records (birth, marriage, death) are a matter for the receiving office’s rules too, and occasionally for the issuing state’s. Georgia’s apostille office, which checks the official’s signature against those on file, recommends a new certified copy if a vital record was issued before 2000. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information)
- An old apostille on a still-acceptable document is fine. If an official refuses it only because the apostille is old, that refusal isn’t consistent with the Convention. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf)
If the receiving office does want a newer document, you need a fresh certified copy (or a new notarization) and a new apostille from the state that issued it; the old apostille can’t be moved onto the new paper, since it only has effect while attached to its own document. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf) Our apostille finder gives the office and fee for each covered state.

## Before you assume it has expired

- Ask the receiving authority what it actually requires. If it wants a recently issued document, that is a rule about the document, not the apostille. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf)
- Check the apostille is still attached and legible, since its effect depends on staying identifiable and attached. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf)
- If the receiving office doubts the apostille is genuine, point it to the issuing office’s register; see how to verify an apostille.
- If the destination isn’t a Hague country at all, the apostille rules don’t apply; see apostille versus authentication and apostille by country.

# How to get an apostille in Arizona
Short answer: Send the original notarized or certified document, the Apostille/Certificate of Authentication Request form, $3 per document, and return postage to the Arizona Secretary of State, Attn: Apostille Dept., 1700 W. Washington Street, Fl. 7, Phoenix, AZ 85007-2808. Mail takes 10 to 20 business days. If you can’t wait, walk-in service costs an extra $25 expedite fee and is limited to 6 documents. [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication)

The Arizona Secretary of State issues an apostille, or for other countries a certificate of authentication, to certify an Arizona notary public, court clerk, or state document custodian. Which one you get depends on the country that asked for it. [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication) The Secretary of State and the Assistant Secretary of State are the officers designated to sign Arizona apostilles under the U.S. designation filed with the Hague Conference. [source](https://www.hcch.net/en/states/authorities/details3/?aid=353)

## Fees, speed, and contact

| Service | Fee | How long |
| By mail | $3 per document [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication) | 10 to 20 business days [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication) |
| Walk-in, Phoenix or Tucson | $3 per document plus a $25 expedite fee; limit of 6 documents [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication) | — |
| Puerto Rico or another U.S. territory | $18 notarial capacity certificate (not an apostille) [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication) | — |

- Mail to: Secretary of State, Attn: Apostille Dept., 1700 W. Washington Street, Fl. 7, Phoenix, AZ 85007-2808 [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication)
- In person, Phoenix: State Capitol Executive Tower, 1700 W. Washington Street, Suite 220 [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication)
- In person, Tucson: Arizona State Complex Building, 400 West Congress, Second Floor, Suite 221 [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication)
- Hours: both offices are open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., except holidays. [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication)
- Payment: check or money order payable to “Arizona Secretary of State.” Don’t send cash by mail. A returned (NSF) payment adds a $25 fee. [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication)
- Questions: 602-542-6187 or 1-800-458-5842, or the apostille email form on the Secretary of State’s site. [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication)
Check before you go in person. The Secretary of State’s apostille page carries two Business Services notices: one says Phoenix went to appointment-only service from November 2, 2026, with booking online, and a later one says normal walk-in service resumed on November 9, 2026, at the Executive Tower, 1700 W. Washington St., 2nd Floor. Both were still posted when we checked on November 28, 2026, so call 602-542-6187 before making the trip. [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication) Couriers can drop filings at the counter only if the documents aren’t in a sealed envelope; sealed envelopes go to the ADOA Mail Room, 1802 W Jackson St, Phoenix, AZ 85007. [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication)

## What Arizona will and won’t apostille

- Originals only. The office must receive an original notarized document or an original certified recorded document. A photocopy isn’t accepted. [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication)
- Arizona documents only. Don’t send a document recorded by another state; the state that produced it has to certify it. Arizona’s own example: a Nevada birth certificate goes to the Nevada Secretary of State. Out-of-state documents are returned to you. [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication)
- No electronic apostilles. Arizona issues paper certificates only. [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication) The HCCH’s November 2026 e-APP chart doesn’t list an Arizona e-Register, so a recipient who wants to confirm an Arizona apostille should contact the Secretary of State directly. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/e8e7549d-e34a-452f-9fa3-cf2241aa4197.pdf) See how to verify an apostille.
- U.S. territories. A document going to Puerto Rico or another U.S. territory gets a notarial capacity certificate for $18, not an apostille. [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication)
- Federal documents. The Secretary of State points federal requests to the U.S. Office of Authentications. [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication) Federal documents are signed by a federal official, and the U.S. designation sends them to the U.S. Department of State. [source](https://www.hcch.net/en/states/authorities/details3/?aid=353) See apostille versus authentication.

## What to send

- The original notarized document, or the original certified copy from the office that recorded it. [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication)
- The completed Apostille/Certificate of Authentication Request form, naming the country where the document will be used. [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication)
- $3 per document by check or money order to “Arizona Secretary of State.” [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication)
- Return postage. The office recommends a trackable service. Any FedEx, UPS, DHL or other return label must show your own mailing address as both the sender and the recipient. [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication)
Arizona’s page says it is a filing agency and can’t give legal advice or interpret statutes. [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication) For which certificate your destination needs, see apostille by country; most Hague members simply take the apostille, and the apostille finder lays out the steps for other states’ documents.

Home › How to verify an apostille
# How to verify an apostille
Short answer: Only the office that issued the apostille can verify it. Look at the apostille for the issuing authority, the date and the certificate number, then search that office’s online register (e-Register) if it has one, or contact the office and ask it to check its register. The Hague Conference itself doesn’t issue, record or verify apostilles. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/6dd54368-bebd-4b10-a078-0a92e5bca40a.pdf) [source](https://www.hcch.net/en/instruments/conventions/specialised-sections/apostille)

Every apostille authority has to keep a register of the apostilles it issues, and at the request of anyone interested it must confirm whether the details on an apostille match that register. You don’t have to explain why you’re asking. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf) Seventeen U.S. authorities have a public online register listed by the Hague Conference. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/e8e7549d-e34a-452f-9fa3-cf2241aa4197.pdf)

## Step by step

- Read the apostille. The certificate names who signed the underlying document and in what capacity (or, for an unsigned document, the authority whose seal is on it), the date of the apostille, the authority that issued it, and its number. Those are the details every register must record. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf)
- Find the issuing office. For a U.S. apostille that is the state office named on the certificate (in most states the Secretary of State), or the U.S. Department of State for a federal document. [source](https://www.hcch.net/en/states/authorities/details3/?aid=353) Our apostille offices by state table lists every designated office.
- Use the e-Register if there is one. If the authority runs an e-Register, its web address is printed on the apostille. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/6dd54368-bebd-4b10-a078-0a92e5bca40a.pdf) The U.S. registers listed by the Hague Conference are in the table below.
- Otherwise, ask the office. Where there is no e-Register, send the request to the authority that issued the apostille and it checks its register manually. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf) Contact details for every competent authority are on the Hague Conference’s authorities pages. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/6dd54368-bebd-4b10-a078-0a92e5bca40a.pdf)

This is the U.S. list from the HCCH e-APP Implementation Chart, the version created November 25, 2026, checked November 28, 2026. The chart is compiled from information the countries send in, so a newly launched register can be missing for a while. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/e8e7549d-e34a-452f-9fa3-cf2241aa4197.pdf)

| Issuing authority | Online register | e-Apostilles |
| Arkansas | Search [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/e8e7549d-e34a-452f-9fa3-cf2241aa4197.pdf) | — |

| Utah (Lieutenant Governor) | Search [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/e8e7549d-e34a-452f-9fa3-cf2241aa4197.pdf) | Issues e-Apostilles (from July 2026) |
| Washington | Search [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/e8e7549d-e34a-452f-9fa3-cf2241aa4197.pdf) | e-Apostille pilot February 12, 2024, to September 30, 2025 |
| West Virginia | Search [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/e8e7549d-e34a-452f-9fa3-cf2241aa4197.pdf) | — |

Some registers cover only apostilles issued after a certain date, and a country may run separate registers for separate authorities. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf) New York, for example, says its online tool covers apostilles and certificates issued on or after April 9, 2013. [source](https://dos.ny.gov/apostille-certificate-authentication) A state that isn’t on the list, such as Arizona or Georgia, can still verify its apostilles on request. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf)

## e-Apostilles
An e-Apostille is an apostille issued and signed in digital form. The Hague Conference says it can’t be refused just because it is electronic and is as valid as a paper apostille in every Contracting Party. [source](https://www.hcch.net/en/instruments/conventions/specialised-sections/apostille) e-Apostilles issued during the state pilot programs in the table are legitimate, validly issued e-Apostilles, not test certificates. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/e8e7549d-e34a-452f-9fa3-cf2241aa4197.pdf) An e-Register can record paper apostilles and e-Apostilles alike. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf)

## What a match does and doesn’t tell you
A matching register entry confirms the apostille was issued as shown. It doesn’t vouch for what the document says: an apostille only certifies the origin of the public document, meaning the signature, the capacity of the signer, and any seal or stamp. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/6dd54368-bebd-4b10-a078-0a92e5bca40a.pdf) The receiving country still decides whether the document itself is acceptable, for example whether it meets its domestic requirements or has been altered. [source](https://assets.hcch.net/docs/a19ae90b-27bf-4596-b5ee-0140858abeaa.pdf) An apostille also can’t be turned down just because it is old; see does an apostille expire?
Not sure your document got the right certificate in the first place? Apostille versus authentication explains which countries take an apostille and which need the longer legalization route, and apostille by country has each Hague member.

# How to get an apostille in Colorado
Short answer: The Colorado Secretary of State, 1700 Broadway, Suite 550, Denver, charges $5 per apostille when you mail or drop off your documents, and $15 per apostille for expedited walk-in service. Pay by check or money order to “Colorado Secretary of State”; cards aren’t accepted. There’s no online apostille. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/notary/forms/NAUTH.pdf) [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/general.html)

Since April 2, 2018, Colorado has issued one combined certificate of authentication. For a country in the Hague Apostille Convention, that certificate serves as the apostille. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/general.html) Colorado won’t issue one for use in the United States or its territories (American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands). [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/notary/forms/NAUTH.pdf)

## Fees, speed, and contact

| Service | Fee | How long |
| Mail in | $5 per apostille [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/notary/forms/NAUTH.pdf) | Worked in the order received. The office says it is seeing longer than normal wait times; mail first goes through a state distribution center. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/general.html) |
| Drop off | $5 per apostille [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/notary/forms/NAUTH.pdf) | The office emails or calls when the documents are ready to pick up. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/general.html) |
| Expedited, walk-in only | $15 per apostille [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/notary/forms/NAUTH.pdf) | Hand-deliver before 4:30 p.m. The office tries to finish while you wait, generally in under an hour, but may ask you to come back when it is busy. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/general.html) |

- Address: Colorado Secretary of State, Authentications Program, 1700 Broadway, Ste. 550, Denver, CO 80290 [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/notary/forms/NAUTH.pdf)
- Walk-in hours for expedited service: 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/info_center/contact.html)
- Payment: check or money order payable to Colorado Secretary of State. The request form also lists cash for in-person service; never mail cash. No credit or debit cards. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/general.html) [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/notary/forms/NAUTH.pdf)
- Contact: 303-894-2200; Authentications@coloradosos.gov [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/notary/forms/NAUTH.pdf)
- Documents aren’t processed on weekends or holidays. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/general.html)

## Which documents Colorado can apostille
The original document must carry at least one of these: a Colorado notary public’s signature, a certification by Colorado Vital Records, or a certification by a Colorado county clerk’s office. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/general.html) The rejection guide adds originals certified by the Colorado Secretary of State or the Colorado State Archives. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/rejectReasons.html) The office doesn’t notarize. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/general.html)

| Your document | Where it comes from |
| Colorado birth or death certificate | A certified copy from the Vital Records Office of Colorado [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/general.html) |
| Marriage license, divorce decree, court documents | Copies from the County Clerk and Recorder or the Clerk of the District Court where they were issued [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/general.html) |
| Business records | Free certified copies from the Secretary of State’s business database (“Get certified copies of documents” on the entity’s summary page). Print in color for official use. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/business.html) |
| Power of attorney, school transcripts, other private documents | Notarized by a Colorado notary public [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/general.html) |
| Certificate of Naturalization | Not Colorado’s. Get a certified true copy from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, then send it to the U.S. Department of State, Office of Authentications. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/general.html) |

For business records, check first whether the receiving country accepts a plain certified copy; Colorado says certified copies generally meet other countries’ requirements. It only adds an apostille to business records for Hague countries. For other countries, the certified copies go to the U.S. Department of State. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/business.html)
Out-of-state records: Colorado can’t authenticate another state’s document, but a Colorado notary can make a certified copy of an out-of-state government document such as a birth certificate or marriage license. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/general.html) A Colorado notary can’t certify a copy of a record you can get from a Colorado clerk and recorder, the Secretary of State, the State Archives, or a vital records office; order a certified copy from that office instead. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/rejectReasons.html)

## Why Colorado rejects documents

- Blanks: every blank must be filled in or crossed out, or the notarization doesn’t comply with Colorado law. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/general.html) [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/rejectReasons.html)
- The notary statement: it needs original signatures and must show the state, the county, and the date of notarization. The document can be in another language, but the notary’s statement must be in English. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/general.html)
- Powers of attorney with legal conclusions: many foreign POAs have the notary state the parties’ legal capacity or say the notary explained the document. Unless the notary is also a Colorado-licensed attorney, that is the unauthorized practice of law, and Colorado will authenticate the POA only if it is revised to fit Colorado law or the notary is a Colorado attorney. The consulate or embassy may be another option. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/rejectReasons.html)
- “Proof of life” certifications: a Colorado notary can’t certify that someone is alive. The person can instead swear to a written statement that they are alive and have that notarized; check that the receiving country accepts it. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/rejectReasons.html)
- I-9 forms: they aren’t notarized and are federal documents. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/rejectReasons.html)
- Certain subjects: Colorado won’t authenticate notarized records about allegiance, renouncing or relinquishing citizenship, sovereignty, “in itinere” status, the World Service Authority, or claimed immunity from state or federal law. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/rejectReasons.html)
Free review first: email a PDF of your document to Authentications@coloradosos.gov and the office will review it and give feedback, within 3 to 5 business days according to its rejection guide. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/general.html) [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/rejectReasons.html) If you plan to notarize online, the notary must be a Colorado notary public for Colorado to authenticate it, so the review is a good way to check the certificate wording first. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/general.html)

## What to send

- The original document. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/general.html)
- The completed Apostilles & Authentications Request Form (a Spanish version is on the program page), naming the country where the documents will be used and the number of apostilles. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/notary/forms/NAUTH.pdf) [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/home.html)
- A check or money order to “Colorado Secretary of State” for $5 per apostille. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/notary/forms/NAUTH.pdf)
- Your return choice: hold for pickup, free standard USPS, or a prepaid FedEx or UPS label. Don’t put the office’s own name or address as the return address on the label, or the documents come back by standard mail. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/notary/forms/NAUTH.pdf)
Receiving an apostille issued in Colorado? You can verify it on the Secretary of State’s site. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/home.html) For the destination country, see apostille by country; for non-Hague countries, see apostille versus authentication.
Rather not do this yourself?
Tell us the document, that it was issued in Colorado, and where it's going. We'll pass your request to an independent apostille service that can handle the whole thing, and they'll reply with a quote. It's free to ask and you're under no obligation.

# How to get an apostille in Georgia
Short answer: In Georgia, apostilles are issued by the Georgia Superior Court Clerks’ Cooperative Authority (GSCCCA), not the Secretary of State. It charges $3 per document. You can walk in at 1875 Century Blvd. in Atlanta, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays with no appointment, or mail your originals; mailed requests normally take one to two business days. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information)

Georgia splits the work between two agencies. The GSCCCA issues apostilles for countries in the Hague Apostille Convention. For a country that isn’t in the Convention, the Georgia Secretary of State issues a Great Seal Certification instead; the GSCCCA can’t. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information) The GSCCCA is the designated apostille authority for Georgia on the Hague Conference’s list for the United States. [source](https://www.hcch.net/en/states/authorities/details3/?aid=353)

## Fees, speed, and contact

| Item | Georgia rule |
| Apostille fee | $3 per document [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information) |
| Walk-in | 1875 Century Blvd., Ste. 100, Atlanta, GA 30345. 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., Monday to Friday, no appointment. Usually under 20 minutes, depending on how many documents you bring; the office may limit how many it handles while you wait. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information) |
| Mail | GSCCCA, Attn: Notary Division, 1875 Century Blvd., Ste. 100, Atlanta, GA 30345. Processing is normally one to two business days. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information) |
| Payment, walk-in | Cash, a check with a pre-printed name and address, or a money order payable to GSCCCA, or a credit card [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information) |
| Payment, mail | A check with a pre-printed name and address or a money order payable to GSCCCA, or the GSCCCA’s credit card pre-payment voucher [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information) |
| Contact | notary@gsccca.org; 404-327-6023 or 800-304-5175 [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information) |
| Non-Hague countries | Great Seal Certification from the Georgia Secretary of State, 404-656-2871 [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information) |

Atlanta is the only place in Georgia that issues apostilles. The GSCCCA doesn’t notarize documents, so arrive with the notarization already done. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information)

## Apostille or Great Seal Certification?
Start with the destination country. If it is on the GSCCCA’s list of participating countries, the document goes to the GSCCCA for an apostille. If it isn’t listed, the country isn’t part of the Apostille Convention and you need the Secretary of State’s Great Seal Certification. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information) A document going to a foreign embassy or consulate inside the United States counts as going to that country. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information)
The GSCCCA also issues a certification of notary public ($2), but that one is only for documents used inside the U.S., a U.S. territory, or a U.S. embassy, typically for visa requests. It is never used together with an apostille. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information) For how the two foreign certificates differ, see apostille versus authentication.

## What Georgia can apostille

| Your document | What it needs |
| Birth or death certificate | An official certified copy from the Georgia Department of Community Health, or a county Probate Court or Health Department, with the issuing official’s signature and seal. Never notarized. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information) |
| Marriage certificate or license | An official certified copy from the county Probate Court [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information) |
| Divorce decree and court documents | An official certified copy from the county Clerk of Superior Court. In counties in the eCertification program, a printed digital certified copy of a divorce decree can be apostilled. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information) |
| Corporate records (articles, certificates) | Certified copies issued by the current Secretary of State, either from the Corporations Division or downloaded from its website [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information) |
| Notarized documents (power of attorney, affidavit, translation, school records) | Notarized by a Georgia notary in line with Georgia law. No county certification is needed before the apostille. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information) |

The GSCCCA checks the official’s signature against the ones it has on file. If your vital record was issued before 2000, it recommends getting a new certified copy, and it prefers copies issued since then. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information) New certified birth and death certificates come from the Georgia Department of Community Health (Vital Records) or the county Probate Court or Health Department. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information)

## What it can’t apostille

- Documents from another state; send them to that state. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information)
- Federal documents signed and sealed by a federal agency or court, including a consular report of birth abroad. These go to the U.S. Department of State. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information)
- Photocopies, unless a Georgia notary has properly certified the copy. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information)
- Foreign documents, documents for non-Hague countries, and documents for use inside the United States. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information)

## What the notarization must show
The notary completes a notarial certificate and signs by hand in ink, using exactly the name on the commission, with the exact date of notarization. The seal must show the notary’s name, the county of commission, the words “Notary Public,” and the state, and the impression has to be clear. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information) Sample certificates are in the GSCCCA’s notary files and forms. If you plan to notarize online, the document still has to be a Georgia notarization for the GSCCCA to apostille it.

## Specific documents

- Transcripts and grades: a school official signs in front of a notary. The simplest route is a short letter from the official saying the attached are the student’s official records. Only Georgia school records can be apostilled in Georgia. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information)
- Diplomas: a Georgia notary can certify a copy of the original as a “true and exact copy of the original,” and the apostille goes on that copy. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information)
- Background checks: an FBI check signed and sealed by an FBI official goes to the U.S. Department of State. A GBI check signed by a GBI official before a notary is ready for the apostille. For an unsigned FBI check or a local police check that wasn’t notarized, you sign the GSCCCA’s Criminal Records Check affidavit before a Georgia notary. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information)
- Translations: the translator signs an affidavit before a Georgia notary saying they know both languages and the translation is true and complete. The notary can’t also be the translator. The original document doesn’t need to be in English. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information)
- Passport copies: a Georgia notary can certify a copy of a U.S. passport using the GSCCCA’s passport affidavit; a foreign passport copy uses its Foreign Passport Affidavit. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information)
- Getting married abroad: there’s no standard U.S. certificate of freedom to marry, and a notarized single status affidavit often works; the GSCCCA has sample language. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information)
- Adoptions: the GSCCCA encourages adoptive parents to contact it before submitting. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information)

## What to put in a mailed request

- The original documents. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information)
- A cover letter or note naming the destination country, with your contact information. The GSCCCA has a sample Apostille Request Letter in its forms. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information)
- $3 per document by check or money order payable to GSCCCA, or a credit card pre-payment voucher. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information)
- A prepaid, self-addressed return envelope or airbill. FedEx and UPS airbills must be computer generated; handwritten ones are not accepted. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information)
For the country itself, see apostille by country, or build your checklist with the apostille finder.
Rather not do this yourself?
Tell us the document, that it was issued in Georgia, and where it's going. We'll pass your request to an independent apostille service that can handle the whole thing, and they'll reply with a quote. It's free to ask and you're under no obligation.

- Apostille-USA, original document
- Apostille-USA, true (certified) copy
See the affiliate disclosure for how those links work.

# How to get an apostille in Minnesota
Short answer: The Minnesota Secretary of State charges $5 per document for an apostille. Mail the documents with the request form and payment to the First National Bank Building, 332 Minnesota Street, Suite N201, Saint Paul, MN 55101, or book an in-person appointment. Birth, marriage, and other certified records go as they are; everything else must be notarized by a Minnesota notary first. [source](https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/2264/authentication-mail-form.pdf)

Minnesota issues only one kind of certificate: the apostille, whatever the destination country. If the receiving country doesn’t accept an apostille, contact that country’s embassy or consulate about your options. [source](https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/2264/authentication-mail-form.pdf) An apostille is for international use only and can’t be used in the United States or its territories. [source](https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/2264/authentication-mail-form.pdf)

## Fees and contact

| Item | Minnesota rule |
| State fee | $5 per document presented. A Minnesota birth certificate plus a three-page notarized transcript is two documents, so $10. [source](https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/2264/authentication-mail-form.pdf) |
| Payment by mail | Personal or business check, cashier’s check, or money order payable to MN Secretary of State, or a charge to a Secretary of State client account. Cash is accepted but mailing it is at your own risk. No credit card or wire payments by mail; U.S. dollars only. [source](https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/2264/authentication-mail-form.pdf) |
| Mailing address | MN Secretary of State, First National Bank Building, 332 Minnesota Street, Suite N201, Saint Paul, MN 55101 [source](https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/2264/authentication-mail-form.pdf) |
| In person | By appointment, booked at sos.mn.gov/appointment [source](https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/2264/authentication-mail-form.pdf) |
| Processing time | — |
| Contact | apostille.oss@state.mn.us; 651-296-2803 [source](https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/2264/authentication-mail-form.pdf) or 1-877-551-6767, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. [source](https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/4253/authentication-mail-form.pdf) |

## Two kinds of documents

| Your document | What it needs |
| State or county certified records: birth and death certificates, marriage certificates, divorce decrees, judgments | No notarization. It must be issued in Minnesota, be the original certified document (most county-issued documents have an embossed seal), and not be a photocopy. [source](https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/2264/authentication-mail-form.pdf) |
| Everything else: adoption papers, affidavits, diplomas, transcripts, powers of attorney | Properly notarized by a Minnesota notary public [source](https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/2264/authentication-mail-form.pdf) |

Documents that originated outside Minnesota are a common reason for rejection, as are private documents that weren’t notarized and documents without an original signature. [source](https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/4253/authentication-mail-form.pdf)

## The six things a Minnesota notarization must show
Minnesota checks notarized documents against Minnesota Statutes 358.65. All six elements must be there: [source](https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/2264/authentication-mail-form.pdf)

- Jurisdiction: where the notarization took place, for example County of Ramsey, State of Minnesota.
- Notarial statement: what the notary witnessed, such as a signature, an oath, or a true copy.
- Title: stated as Notary Public.
- Date of the notarization.
- Notary signature in wet ink, not a photocopy.
- Notary stamp.
A missing certificate and an invalid notary commission, including a stamp that doesn’t match, are the notarization problems the office lists most often. [source](https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/4253/authentication-mail-form.pdf) If you plan to notarize online, choose a notary commissioned in Minnesota, because documents must be notarized by a Minnesota notary public. [source](https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/2264/authentication-mail-form.pdf)

## What to put in a mailed request

- The Apostille/Authentication Request Form, with the number of documents (you need one document for each apostille). [source](https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/2264/authentication-mail-form.pdf)
- The original certified or notarized documents. [source](https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/2264/authentication-mail-form.pdf)
- $5 per document, payable to MN Secretary of State. [source](https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/2264/authentication-mail-form.pdf)
- Your return choice. You can pick up from the office, but payment must be in the envelope (you can’t pay at pickup), and if you don’t confirm within three business days the order is mailed by regular U.S. mail. Otherwise enclose a prepaid return envelope, or the documents come back by regular U.S. mail, which has no tracking. [source](https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/2264/authentication-mail-form.pdf)
The Secretary of State is the designated apostille authority for Minnesota on the Hague Conference’s list for the United States. [source](https://www.hcch.net/en/states/authorities/details3/?aid=353) For the destination country, see apostille by country, and for countries outside the Convention, see apostille versus authentication.
Rather not do this yourself?
Tell us the document, that it was issued in Minnesota, and where it's going. We'll pass your request to an independent apostille service that can handle the whole thing, and they'll reply with a quote. It's free to ask and you're under no obligation.

# Apostille versus authentication
Short answer: Use an apostille when the destination country is a party to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention; one certificate replaces the longer legalization chain. For other countries, U.S. states usually issue an authentication or certification instead, and the U.S. Department of State or the country's embassy or consulate may need to add a further step. [source](https://www.hcch.net/en/instruments/conventions/specialised-sections/apostille)

The paper you need depends on the destination country, and on which U.S. office issued or notarized the document. States do not all use the same certificate for non-Hague countries.
To see which certificate your document needs and the steps for your state, use the apostille finder.

## What is an apostille?
The Convention of 5 October 1961 Abolishing the Requirement of Legalisation for Foreign Public Documents — the HCCH 1961 Apostille Convention — is meant to replace the traditional, often long legalization chain with a single apostille issued by a competent authority in the place where the document originates. [source](https://www.hcch.net/en/instruments/conventions/specialised-sections/apostille) The HCCH Apostille Section, checked November 22, 2026, stated that the Convention has 130 Contracting Parties. [source](https://www.hcch.net/en/instruments/conventions/specialised-sections/apostille)
The current list of Contracting Parties is maintained by the Hague Conference. We do not reproduce that list here because it changes when countries join. Check the official HCCH status table for the country that will receive the document.
The HCCH also notes that only designated competent authorities of Contracting Parties may issue or verify apostilles, and that an e-Apostille (an apostille issued in digital form) cannot be refused simply because it is electronic. [source](https://www.hcch.net/en/instruments/conventions/specialised-sections/apostille) Whether a particular U.S. state issues e-apostilles is a separate question; none of the five state pages reviewed for this site advertised an e-apostille option on the date we checked.

## What is an authentication certificate?
When the destination country is not a party to the Apostille Convention, U.S. offices often issue a different certificate, sometimes called a certificate of authentication or a notarial certification. That certificate may not finish the process: the destination country may still require legalization by its embassy or consulate, and some U.S. states say a further certification from the U.S. Department of State may be required first.
We were not able to load the live U.S. Department of State authentications pages from this research environment (the site returned a Cloudflare block). We therefore do not quote a federal fee or federal processing time. For federal documents, and for any extra State Department step after a state authentication, use the official pages: Authenticate Your Document and the Office of Authentications.

## Which certificate does each state issue?

| State | What the official page says |
| New York | An apostille is issued for use in countries that have joined the 1961 Hague Convention. A Certificate of Authentication is issued for use in a country that is not a member. Certificates of Authentication “may also require an additional certification from the United States Department of State prior to submission to the foreign country.” [source](https://dos.ny.gov/apostille-certificate-authentication) |
| California | The California Secretary of State “issues a single Apostille for documents to be used outside of the United States, regardless of the country of destination.” It does not issue a separate authentication certificate. [source](https://www.sos.ca.gov/notary/apostille-faqs) |
| Texas | Texas issues a “universal Apostille.” It “operates as an apostille for countries that are party to the Apostille Convention and operates as an authentication for countries that are not.” If the destination country is not a party, Texas says you “likely need to get your universal Apostille validated by the Office of Authentications with the U.S. State Department.” [source](https://www.sos.state.tx.us/authfaqs.shtml) |
| Florida | Florida issues an apostille for Hague Convention member states. “Countries that are nonmembers of the 1961 Hague Convention are not issued an apostille; they are issued notarial certificates or certifications.” [source](https://dos.fl.gov/sunbiz/other-services/apostille-notarial-certification/faq) |
| Massachusetts | “If the country is a signatory to the Hague Convention, the document will be called an apostille.” The office issues certifications and apostilles, and the official page tells you to identify the destination country because “different countries require different types of certification.” [source](https://www.sec.state.ma.us/divisions/commissions/apostilles.htm) |
| New Jersey | The Division of Revenue and Enterprise Services provides an apostille if the country subscribes to the Hague Convention. If the country is not on the Hague list, it provides a certification of the public official. [source](https://www.nj.gov/treasury/revenue/apostilles.shtml) |
| Virginia | “Depending on the destination country, the authentication is issued either as a Great Seal or an Apostille.” [source](https://www.commonwealth.virginia.gov/official-documents/authentications/) |
| North Carolina | Three certificates: an Apostille for Hague countries; an Authentication for North Carolina government-issued documents going to non-Hague countries; and an Authority for documents notarized in North Carolina going to non-Hague countries. [source](https://www.sosnc.gov/frequently_asked_questions/by_title/_Authentications) |
| Pennsylvania | The destination country determines whether the authentication is an Apostille or a Certification. Pennsylvania now prints both on a single universal certificate; a certification may still need the U.S. Department of State and the foreign embassy. [source](https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dos/programs/document-certification) |
| Missouri | A certification verifies a notary; an authentication verifies recorders of deeds, circuit clerks, judges, county clerks, and the State Registrar; an apostille is issued for Hague Convention countries. [source](https://www.sos.mo.gov/Business/Notary/notary/certify) |
| Washington | One “universal certificate” serves as an Apostille for Hague countries or an Authentication for non-member countries, which may also need the U.S. Department of State, the embassy, or both. [source](https://www.sos.wa.gov/corporations-charities/apostilles-services-information-resource-page) |
| Michigan | An Apostille for Hague countries and a Certificate of Authority for all others, with the same requirements and fee. Many non-Hague countries also want a federal-level certification. [source](https://www.michigan.gov/sos/all-services/document-authentication-and-apostille) |
| Connecticut | An Apostille for Hague countries and an Authentication for others, which may need further legalization by the U.S. Department of State or the embassy. Connecticut also issues e-Apostilles for eligible documents, but not for vital records. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille) |
| Maryland | An Apostille for Hague countries and a standard certification for others; a standard certification then goes to the U.S. Department of State before the embassy. [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/Pages/default.aspx) |
| Georgia | Two agencies: the GSCCCA issues apostilles for Hague countries; the Secretary of State issues a Great Seal Certification for all others. [source](https://www.gsccca.org/notary-and-apostilles/apostilles/general-apostille-information) |
| Colorado | One combined certificate of authentication since April 2, 2018, which serves as an apostille in Hague countries. [source](https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/apostilles/general.html) |
| Minnesota | Only an apostille, whatever the destination. If the country doesn’t accept apostilles, contact its embassy or consulate about options. [source](https://www.sos.mn.gov/media/2264/authentication-mail-form.pdf) |
| Arizona | An Apostille or a certificate of Authentication, depending on the country that requested it. Arizona issues paper certificates only, no electronic apostilles. [source](https://azsos.gov/business/authentication) |

## Who authenticates federal and out-of-state documents?
State apostille offices generally authenticate only that state’s public documents or documents notarized by that state’s notaries. New York says Federal/FBI background checks must be authenticated by the U.S. Department of State. [source](https://dos.ny.gov/apostille-certificate-authentication) Florida says federal documents should be submitted to the U.S. Department of State, and that a document issued or notarized in another state should go to that state’s competent authority. [source](https://dos.fl.gov/sunbiz/other-services/apostille-notarial-certification) Massachusetts says it does not certify out-of-state documents; they must be certified by the state of origin. [source](https://www.sec.state.ma.us/divisions/commissions/download/apostille_and_certification_information.pdf)
The federal fee and the current Office of Authentications process are not quoted here. Use the official State Department pages linked above.
If you'd rather have a service handle a federal (U.S. Department of State) apostille, one option is Apostille-USA. See the affiliate disclosure.

## Official sources

- HCCH Apostille Section
- HCCH status table (Contracting Parties)
- U.S. Department of State, Authenticate Your Document

# How to get an apostille in Connecticut
Short answer: Order online through the Connecticut Secretary of the State’s apostille system; paper order forms are no longer accepted. For a paper apostille you then mail or courier the original to Hartford, and regular orders are processed within 5 to 7 business days of arrival. Eligible documents can get an e-Apostille instead, processed within 24 hours. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille) The fee set by law is $40 per document, or $15 for documents connected with a child’s adoption, and an e-Apostille costs the same as paper. [source](https://prdext2.cga.ct.gov/2026/sum/pdf/2026SUM00081-R01SB-00294-SUM.pdf)

The Secretary of the State issues an apostille for Hague Apostille Convention countries and an authentication for other countries, which may then need the U.S. Department of State or the destination country’s embassy. Since July 21, 2025, Connecticut uses a single authentication certificate for all legalization requests. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille)

## Fees and processing times

| Service | Fee | Processing time |
| Paper apostille or authentication, regular | $40 per document [source](https://prdext2.cga.ct.gov/2026/sum/pdf/2026SUM00081-R01SB-00294-SUM.pdf) | Within 5 to 7 business days of receipt [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille) |
| Adoption-related document | $15 per document [source](https://prdext2.cga.ct.gov/2026/sum/pdf/2026SUM00081-R01SB-00294-SUM.pdf) | — |
| Expedited paper order | — | Within 24 hours of receipt [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille) |
| e-Apostille | Same as paper [source](https://prdext2.cga.ct.gov/2026/sum/pdf/2026SUM00081-R01SB-00294-SUM.pdf) | Within 24 hours (one business day) of a complete application [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille) |

Fees are from the Office of Legislative Research summary of Public Act 26-81, which sets the per-document fee for apostilles and authentications. [source](https://prdext2.cga.ct.gov/2026/sum/pdf/2026SUM00081-R01SB-00294-SUM.pdf) The online system shows your total when you order. [source](https://sots.service.ct.gov/apostille/) Postage and courier costs are yours.

## Step by step

- Prepare the document. Use an original or a certified copy. It must be notarized by a Connecticut notary or certified by a Connecticut official, within the last 10 years, with an original signature and/or seal. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille)
- Order online. Go to sots.service.ct.gov/apostille, create an account, log in, and place the order. All orders must be submitted online. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille)
- e-Apostille: upload the document to be processed digitally. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille)
- Paper apostille: mail the original or certified document with your printed order receipt (or your APO Work Order number) and a prepaid, pre-addressed return envelope or shipping label. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille)
- Track it in your online account, which has real-time order tracking and secure messaging. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille)

## Where to send paper orders

| Method | Address |
| FedEx, UPS, DHL, or hand delivery (the office calls this the preferred method) | Secretary of the State, Authentications and Apostilles, 165 Capitol Avenue, Suite 1000, Hartford, CT 06106 [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille) |
| U.S. Postal Service (slower) | Secretary of the State, Authentications and Apostilles, P.O. Box 150470, Hartford, CT 06115-0470 [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille) |

If you include a prepaid FedEx, UPS, DHL, or USPS label, the document comes back that way; otherwise it is returned by first-class mail. International return shipping needs a prepaid label. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille)

## Paper apostille or e-Apostille?

| | Paper apostille | e-Apostille |
| What you get | A physical certificate attached to the original [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille) | A secure electronic certificate you download [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille) |
| Speed | 5 to 7 business days; 24 hours if expedited [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille) | One business day from a complete application [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille) |
| Vital records (birth, death, marriage, adoption certificates) | Required [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille) | Not eligible [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille) |
| Printing | — | Not valid if printed [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille) |

Connecticut began issuing e-Apostilles on July 6, 2026, and not every document type is eligible yet. e-Apostilles are accepted by Hague Convention members, but the office suggests confirming with the receiving agency or institution before you order. Anyone can check a Connecticut paper apostille or e-Apostille on the verification portal. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille)

## What Connecticut can authenticate
Only documents signed by a Connecticut public official: Connecticut notaries public; town clerks and their assistants and deputies; local registrars of vital statistics and their assistants and deputies; clerks and assistant clerks of the Superior and Probate Courts; commissioners of Connecticut state agencies; and justices of the peace. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille)

| Document | Connecticut rule |
| Birth, death, marriage certificates | A certified copy from the town clerk or the Department of Public Health Vital Records Unit, with a paper apostille. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille) See how to obtain a record. |
| Copies of documents | A copy can be authenticated if it comes with a written statement that it is true and accurate, sworn to and signed before a Connecticut notary. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille) |
| Court records | Signed by a clerk or assistant clerk of the Superior or Probate Court. Out-of-state court documents go to the issuing state. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille) |
| School transcripts | Connecticut schools only; out-of-state transcripts are authenticated by the state where the school is. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille) |
| Federal documents (for example, FBI checks) | Not Connecticut’s; they go to the U.S. Department of State. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille) |

## What Connecticut won’t authenticate

- Documents signed by an out-of-state notary. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille)
- Documents executed by an attorney signing as a Commissioner of the Superior Court. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille)
- Out-of-state vital records, court documents, and school transcripts. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille)
- Documents to be presented in a U.S. territory such as Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa, or the Northern Mariana Islands. Territories aren’t foreign jurisdictions, so a properly notarized or Connecticut-issued document can be used there without a certificate. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille)

## Getting the notarization right
Because the notary must be commissioned in Connecticut, a notarization by a notary from another state won’t work. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille) Connecticut notaries may charge up to $10 per notarial act since July 1, 2026, and Connecticut has allowed remote notarial acts since October 1, 2023. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/business-services/notary/notary-public-licensing) If you use online notarization, make sure the notary holds a Connecticut commission.

## Contact
Email BSD@ct.gov or call 860-509-6002 (option 4), Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. [source](https://portal.ct.gov/sots/legislative-services/authentication-of-documents-and-the-apostille)
Rather not do this yourself?
Tell us the document, that it was issued in Connecticut, and where it's going. We'll pass your request to an independent apostille service that can handle the whole thing, and they'll reply with a quote. It's free to ask and you're under no obligation.

Last updated: 2026-11-25

# How to get an apostille in Maryland
Short answer: The Maryland Secretary of State’s Certification Desk in Annapolis charges $5 per document for an apostille or a standard certification. Mail is the dependable route right now: walk-in service is not available, scheduled appointments are subject to change because of building construction, and the office says it will move to mail-in only once construction begins. If the document is notarized, take it to the Clerk of the Circuit Court in the notary’s county first. [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/Pages/default.aspx)

Maryland issues an apostille for countries in the Hague Convention and a standard certification for all others. A standard certification then goes to the U.S. Department of State, Office of Authentications, before the destination country’s embassy. [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/Pages/default.aspx)

## Fees, speed, and contact

| Item | Maryland rule |
| State fee | $5 per document. By mail, pay by U.S. check or U.S. money order made out to the Secretary of State, one payment per order (don’t staple the check). In person you can also pay by credit or debit card. [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/Pages/default.aspx) [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/SiteAssets/Pages/default/check%20list%20FOR%20DOCUMENTS%20to%20be%20certified1.pdf) |
| Processing, FedEx and UPS | Around 3 to 4 days [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/Pages/default.aspx) |
| Processing, USPS Priority Mail | Up to 3 to 4 days [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/Pages/default.aspx) |
| Processing, regular mail | 7 to 14 business days [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/Pages/default.aspx) |
| Mailing address | Certification Desk, Office of the Secretary of State, 16 Francis Street, 1st floor, Annapolis, MD 21401 [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/SiteAssets/Pages/default/check%20list%20FOR%20DOCUMENTS%20to%20be%20certified1.pdf) |
| In person | 16 Francis Street, Wineland Building, Annapolis. Hours 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., Monday to Friday, closed on Maryland state holidays. Walk-in service is not available; appointments are booked online, are limited to 10 documents per customer per day, and space is limited to two family members. [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/Pages/default.aspx) |
| Phone and email | 410-974-5521; DLCertifications_sos@maryland.gov [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/Pages/default.aspx) |

Check the Secretary of State’s page or call before you travel; the office posts closures and appointment changes there. [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/Pages/default.aspx) Appointments are booked through the Secretary of State front desk booking page.

## The two routes

| Your document | Steps |
| Notarized document (power of attorney, affidavit, consent, school record) | 1. Take it to the Clerk of the Circuit Court in the county where the notary was commissioned (the county is on the notary’s seal). 2. Send it to the Secretary of State in Annapolis. [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/Pages/default.aspx) |
| State or county document (birth or death certificate, marriage certificate, divorce decree, criminal record status certification, motor vehicle ownership certification) | Send it straight to the Secretary of State, as long as it carries the seal and authorized signature of the issuing department. No circuit court step. If your copy isn’t current, call 410-974-5521 first to confirm it can be authenticated. [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/Pages/default.aspx) |
| Federal document (FBI background check, USCIS documents, birth abroad certificates) | Not Maryland’s. Submit it directly to the U.S. Department of State. Naturalization and immigration documents can’t be notarized, originals or copies. [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/Pages/default.aspx) |

For a Hague country, the Secretary of State’s apostille is the last step; the document doesn’t go to the U.S. Department of State. For a non-Hague country, it goes to the U.S. Department of State after the Maryland certificate. [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/Pages/default.aspx)

## What does the circuit court step cost?
Each county’s Clerk of the Circuit Court handles its own certification. In Montgomery County, for example, the Circuit Court’s License Department (50 Maryland Avenue, North Tower, Room 1300, Rockville) charges $1, with no appointment needed. [source](https://www.montgomerycountymd.gov/circuit-court/how-do-i/apostille-standard-certification-documents-international-use) Check with the clerk in your notary’s county for its fee and hours. If the clerk who certified your document isn’t the current clerk, call the Secretary of State to confirm it can still be authenticated. [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/Pages/default.aspx)

## Diplomas and transcripts
School records follow the notarized-document route. Schools often send records in a sealed envelope marked not to open. Take the sealed envelope to a notary, who opens it and notarizes the school record. Then the Clerk of the Circuit Court in the notary’s county certifies that the notary is in good standing, and the record goes to the Secretary of State. [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/Pages/default.aspx) If you have the record notarized online, the circuit court step still has to happen in the county where that notary is commissioned, so a Maryland-commissioned notary keeps this simple.

## What to put in a mailed request

- The documents, already certified by the circuit court where needed. [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/Pages/default.aspx)
- The mailing checklist: your name, address, daytime phone, email, and the country where the documents will be used. [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/SiteAssets/Pages/default/check%20list%20FOR%20DOCUMENTS%20to%20be%20certified1.pdf)
- A check or money order to the Secretary of State for $5 per document. [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/SiteAssets/Pages/default/check%20list%20FOR%20DOCUMENTS%20to%20be%20certified1.pdf)
- A postage-paid, self-addressed return envelope, or a prepaid FedEx or UPS envelope. Keep your tracking numbers. [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/SiteAssets/Pages/default/check%20list%20FOR%20DOCUMENTS%20to%20be%20certified1.pdf)

## Things to know

- The Secretary of State can’t guarantee that a foreign country will accept the document; confirm requirements with the receiving office first. [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/Pages/default.aspx)
- The Secretary of State’s authority to certify comes from State Government Article, §7-106. [source](https://sos.maryland.gov/Certifications/Pages/default.aspx)
For the difference between the two certificates, see apostille versus authentication; for the destination country, see apostille by country.
